launcher:intro:
Find a Ze command without memorizing the tree
  =============================================

  You know the task but not the exact command path. Ze's launcher finds
  it as you type.

  We will open the launcher, filter the show commands down to traceroute,
  step back to the root, and find the doctor readiness check.

  Type to filter. Enter drills down. Escape steps back.
launcher:recap:
GENERATED FROM THE LIVE COMMAND REGISTRY
  ========================================

  Type to filter. Enter drills down. Escape moves back.

  The launcher is generated from Ze's live command registry, so it stays
  aligned with the commands available in the installed binary.

  Recording complete.
cli-dashboard:intro:
Inspect live BGP sessions from the CLI
  ======================================

  You want to check active BGP sessions without leaving the terminal or
  standing up a separate monitoring stack.

  We will connect over Ze's SSH management plane, open the continuously
  refreshed BGP dashboard, sort the peer table, and open one session in
  detail.

  s sorts. Arrows move. Enter opens detail. Escape returns.
cli-dashboard:recap:
ONE LIVE VIEW OF EVERY SESSION
  ==============================

  One interactive view combines peer state, uptime, message counters,
  update rates, and per-session detail. The data refreshes while you work.

  Recording complete.
zefs-config:intro:
Configure Ze from storage to live commit
  ========================================

  You are setting up a new router and need the whole path, from creating
  the configuration store to committing a change on the running daemon.

  We will create a fresh ZeFS database with ze init, list and validate
  the stored configuration, connect to Ze's SSH editor, change a setting,
  review the diff, commit, and confirm it live.
zefs-config:ssh:
STORAGE CHECK COMPLETE
  ======================

  ZeFS now contains a valid active configuration.

  Next: connect over SSH and show bgp in its default text format.
  Then switch the default to table, review and commit the diff.
  Return to operational mode and run the same show command again.
zefs-config:recap:
FROM ZE INIT TO A LIVE COMMIT
  =============================

  ze init created the ZeFS database. The same BGP summary changed from
  text to a box-drawing table after the SSH editor committed the new
  default. show | compare exposed the exact change.

  No configuration file was edited on the running router.

  Recording complete.
rib-fib:intro:
Follow one route from control plane to Linux
  ============================================

  You want to see Ze do real routing work, taking a BGP route all the
  way into the Linux forwarding table.

  We will inject 198.51.100.0/24 into the BGP RIB, inspect best-path
  selection, and verify the kernel FIB that netlink programmed.
rib-fib:recap:
ROUTE INSTALLATION PATH
  =======================

  request bgp rib inject
      -> BGP best path
      -> system RIB
      -> Linux kernel FIB

  The automated validator also withdrew the prefix and proved kernel removal.
  Control-plane and kernel state came from the running system.

  Recording complete.
config-views:intro:
One configuration model, views for humans and automation
  ========================================================

  The same YANG-backed configuration can be presented as:

    hierarchical  Compact Junos-style blocks for operators
    set           One complete path per line for scripts and reviews

  We will render one peer both ways, convert set syntax back to blocks,
  and prove the round trip produces identical canonical set commands.

  Then ze pipe will filter and count the live plugin registry.
config-views:recap:
ONE MODEL, TWO PRESENTATIONS
  ============================

  Hierarchical config -> set commands -> hierarchical config
                                |
                                +-> identical canonical set output

  ze pipe composed match and count without a separate jq dependency.
  Every frame was generated from Ze's parser and plugin registry.

  Recording complete.
health-reports:intro:
Diagnose current conditions and recent events
  =============================================

  You are triaging a router and need three different answers from one
  CLI:

    show health    Is every registered component operational?
    show warnings  What needs attention right now?
    show errors    What happened recently?

  A deliberately stale prefix-data date creates a live warning. An
  administrative reset then creates a retained BGP error event.
health-reports:recap:
ONE OPERATIONAL VIEW, PRECISE SEMANTICS
  =======================================

  Health    aggregate component status
  Warnings  current state, cleared automatically
  Errors    immutable recent events

  The SSH login banner and filtered commands read the same report bus.
  Structured codes and details make every signal scriptable.

  Recording complete.
rbac:intro:
Enforce read-only access for a NOC account
  ==========================================

  Your NOC team needs to observe the router but must never change its
  state, even by mistake. The read-only profile allows run commands
  except debug and clear, and denies every edit.

  We will show the profile and its NOC binding, run show version as the
  NOC user, then ask the same user to clear interface counters and watch
  Ze refuse it.

  Passwords are injected outside the recording.
rbac:deny:
Next: test the denied path
  ==========================

  The profile denies every command matching the "clear" prefix.

  Ze resolves the command first, then checks the profile, and refuses
  before the command runs. The response names the reason explicitly:
  "command restricted by access control".
rbac:recap:
THE DAEMON ENFORCES THE PROFILE
  ===============================

  The same authenticated user could run show version but could not clear
  interface counters. Authorization is enforced by the daemon, not by
  shell policy, and a refusal is reported as such rather than as a typo.

  Recording complete.
traceroute:intro:
Trace a live path without the Internet
  ======================================

  You need to check reachability and per-hop latency from the router
  itself, with no dependency on a public looking glass or DNS.

  We will probe 192.0.2.53 through an isolated Linux namespace router,
  show the path once as an operational command, then monitor per-hop
  loss and latency over several rounds.

  The lab uses documentation addresses only.
traceroute:recap:
REAL PROBES THROUGH AN ISOLATED LAB
  ===================================

  Ze sent real ICMP probes through the isolated lab and measured every hop.
  The live view continuously updated loss, latency, and variation without
  contacting any third-party service.

  Recording complete.
host-inventory:intro:
Inspect an unfamiliar Linux host before Ze starts
  =================================================

  You need the kernel, CPU topology, and memory headroom, but the Ze
  daemon is not running yet.

  We will run the commands directly and keep every field in the output.
  YAML makes the complete structured inventory readable in the terminal.
host-inventory:recap:
STRUCTURED INVENTORY, AVAILABLE OFFLINE
  =======================================

  The same command surface reported kernel, CPU, and memory inventory.
  Every field stayed structured data, shown here as YAML and ready to
  feed fleet automation unchanged.

  Recording complete.
config-graph:intro:
Know which peers inherit a group before changing it
  ===================================================

  You need to change the transit group's remote ASN. Before scheduling
  maintenance, you need the exact peers that inherit that value.

  We will inspect and validate the config, then filter Ze's machine-readable
  dependency graph to expose the complete group-to-peer blast radius.
config-graph:recap:
CONFIGURATION AS AN EXPLICIT GRAPH
  ==================================

  The BGP section contained a transit group. Both upstream peers inherited
  from it. The JSON graph exposed these relationships for operators,
  automation, and agent impact analysis.

  Recording complete.
topic-rpki:lab:
Validate routes already on this router
  =====================================

  Ze peers with transit AS 65001. A local test RTR cache supplies VRPs.
  A VRP names a prefix, maximum length and authorized origin ASN.
  We add RPKI live, without reconnecting transit or restarting Ze.
topic-rpki:overview:
Three sections, one live candidate
  =================================

  1. Connect the RTR cache
  2. Choose validation actions
  3. Attach validation to transit

  FRR calls these rpki cache tcp and route-map match rpki.
  Here we load all three sections, compare, then commit once.
topic-rpki:cache:
Connect the RTR cache
  =====================

  This isolated lab uses trusted TCP to 127.0.0.3:3323.
  The cache supplies test data, not public RPKI validation.
  Its two-second refresh makes a failed poll visible in this lab.
topic-rpki:policy:
Choose validation actions
  =========================

  Valid means the origin and prefix length match a VRP.
  NotFound means no VRP covers the route. We accept both.
  Invalid stays visible in Adj-RIB-In, but cannot be selected.
topic-rpki:attach:
Attach validation to transit
  ============================

  Add the receive binding to the already established transit peer.
  Route Refresh was negotiated at boot; no RPKI binding was in the base.
  Retained routes are revalidated. The external speaker must see one connection.
topic-rpki:proof:
Read the validation result
  =========================

  9.43.0.0/24 is Valid. 11.43.0.0/24 is NotFound.
  10.43.0.0/24 is Invalid and ineligible, not silently deleted.
  Status and summary describe the cache and active validation.
topic-rpki:origin:
Explain the Invalid route
  =========================

  Transit announced origin AS 65001. The covering VRP names AS 65099.
  show bgp rpki roa exposes that mismatch.
  Correct the real authorization or announcement, not the rejection policy.
topic-rpki:failure:
Stop the cache, not the router
  =============================

  Capture a log boundary, then stop only the RTR test service.
  A newer warning proves this outage, beside cache and status.
  FRR's related diagnostic is show rpki cache-connection.
topic-rpki:recovery:
Restore service and prove a new sync
  ===================================

  Idle is Ze's transport state between polls, not proof of an outage.
  Synced VRPs remain usable until their lease expires.
  Restart the cache. Sync must be newer than this outage's failed poll.
topic-irr:lab:
An import list built from registry data
  ======================================

  Ze has a customer peer in AS 65001. This IRR server is a local test server.
  AS-TEST contains 10.0.0.0/24, not 192.168.0.0/24.
  Like bgpq4 -J -l CUSTOMER AS-CUSTOMER for Junos prefix-lists,
  Ze expands an AS-SET, but refreshes its import list inside the router.
topic-irr:overview:
Load the customer's import policy live
  =====================================

  1. Point Ze at the IRR server
  2. Name the customer's AS-SET
  3. Filter the customer's routes with it

  Later: Select the wrong AS-SET, then restore the correct set.
  Each section has its own explanation in the same SSH candidate.
topic-irr:server:
Point Ze at the IRR server
  ==========================

  Query the local test server at 127.0.0.1:4343.
  Refresh its registry data every hour. No public service is contacted.
topic-irr:as-set:
Name the customer's AS-SET
  ==========================

  AS-TEST expands to the prefixes this customer may announce.
  The peer's session names the set. We also use this section to repair it.
topic-irr:import:
Filter the customer's routes with it
  ===================================

  bgp-filter-irr:65001 selects the list for customer AS 65001.
  A route outside it is rejected at ingress, before Adj-RIB-In.
topic-irr:wrong:
Select the wrong AS-SET
  ======================

  AS-V4ONLY is a real test object, but belongs to another network.
  Its 192.0.2.0/24 list does not authorize this customer's 10.0.0.0/24.
topic-irr:proof:
Check the list and the received routes
  =====================================

  The check command explains a decision, not receipt of an UPDATE.
  The final accepted 10.0.1.0/24 control proves the earlier routes were processed.
  The customer route is present. Its outside prefix and 192.0.2.0/24 are absent.
topic-irr:failure:
A valid object can still be the wrong policy
  ==========================================

  Commit another AS-SET. Clear the old session before reannouncing.
  The final 192.0.2.0/24 control is accepted; both 10.0 routes are absent.
  The intended customer route is refused, not merely late. Ze stays running.
topic-irr:recovery:
Repair the reference, then refresh and announce
  =============================================

  Restore AS-TEST live, run update bgp irr as-set, then reannounce.
  After old routes clear, 10.0.0.0/24 and its 10.0.1.0/24 control must return.
  The wrong-set control and outside prefix must be absent.
topic-commit-confirmed:lab:
A safety window for a remote change
  ==================================

  This running Ze starts as edge-original. We use its actual SSH editor.
  Junos commit confirmed uses minutes and confirms with commit.
  Ze uses seconds and commit accept. Here the window is eight seconds.
topic-commit-confirmed:overview:
Change a live router with a safety net
  =====================================

  1. A trial hostname nobody confirms
  2. A confirmed hostname that stays

  Compare before committing. Watch the first change become active.
  Then deliberately leave it unconfirmed and inspect the rollback.
topic-commit-confirmed:trial:
A trial hostname nobody confirms
  ================================

  Load edge-trial into this candidate and commit confirmed 15.
  We deliberately do not accept it. Ze must restore edge-original.
  This harmless change demonstrates the same safety window as a risky edit.
topic-commit-confirmed:confirmed:
A confirmed hostname that stays
  ===============================

  The hostname is restored and compare shows no pending changes.
  Now load edge-confirmed, commit on probation and run commit accept.
  Wait beyond its fifteen seconds: this change must remain.
topic-commit-confirmed:recap:
Recovery and acceptance are different outcomes
  =============================================

  The unaccepted change restored edge-original on the running router.
  The accepted change stayed edge-confirmed after its deadline.
  History records the revisions. Ze was never restarted.
topic-bfd:overview:
Protect an existing BGP peer with BFD
  =====================================

  The lab is one running Ze router and an FRR peer at 172.29.0.2.
  BGP is already Established. BFD is not configured or bound to it.

  We load two sections in one SSH candidate, compare, then commit:

    1. Set the BFD detection profile
    2. Bind the existing BGP peer

  Then cut the FRR link, inspect why BGP leaves Established, and
  restore the link. The shown Ze process stays running.
topic-bfd:profile:
Set the BFD detection profile
  =============================

  BFD exchanges small control packets to detect a failed path before
  BGP's longer hold timer expires. This profile requests 300 ms packets
  and a detection multiplier of three.

  FRR calls these transmit-interval 300, receive-interval 300 and
  detect-multiplier 3. Ze's desired-min-tx-us and required-min-rx-us
  use microseconds: 300000 is the same requested interval.
topic-bfd:peer:
Bind the existing BGP peer
  ==========================

  A profile alone protects no session. This section opts the existing
  frr BGP peer into single-hop BFD and selects the fast profile.

  FRR: neighbor 172.29.0.1 bfd profile fast
  Ze:  bgp peer frr connection bfd { enabled true; profile fast; }

  The live binding must not replace Ze or reconnect an established BGP
  session merely to enable BFD.
topic-bfd:proof:
Read the live session, not just the configuration
  =================================================

  FRR's show bfd peers corresponds to Ze's show bfd sessions.
  For one peer, use show bfd session address 172.29.0.2.

  Look for Up, packet counts and the selected fast profile. BGP detail
  also shows the negotiated hold timer: that is the deadline against
  which the link-failure observation is measured.
topic-bfd:failure:
Cut the path and inspect the cause
  ==================================

  Bring frr0 down, leaving the shown Ze process alive.

  The readiness check requires the BFD Up-to-Down transition with
  control-detection-time-expired and a BGP Cease / BFD Down notification
  (code 6, subcode 10), before the negotiated hold timer expires.

  The next commands show the retained BFD transition and BGP history.
topic-bfd:fix:
Restore the failed path
  =======================

  BGP releases its BFD session after the failure. Ze retains it briefly
  in AdminDown, then retires it; an empty session list is not a repair.

  Bring the same link up. Recovery requires both a live BFD Up session
  with packet exchange and BGP Established again.
topic-bfd:recap:
One live binding, one diagnosed link failure
  ============================================

  Profile and peer opt-in were loaded in one SSH candidate.
  The evidence comes from actual BFD transitions and the BGP peer,
  not a canned timer message. Restoring the link restores both sessions.

  The PID printed before and after belongs to the same shown Ze process.
topic-ospf:overview:
Follow OSPF from Hello to a usable route
  ========================================

  Ze and FRR share frr0 on 172.29.0.0/24. FRR advertises loopback
  10.255.1.2/32. Ze initially has no OSPF configuration.

  We explain these sections as they are loaded and committed:

    1. Give the router an area
    2. Match the shared-link timers
    3. Introduce a Hello mismatch
    4. Restore the matching Hello interval

  The last two are deliberate live changes after the initial proof.
topic-ospf:area:
Give the router an area
  =======================

  The router ID identifies Ze in OSPF; it is not a new interface address.
  Area 0.0.0.0 is the backbone shared with FRR.

  This section enables the OSPF configuration with router ID 192.0.2.1
  and declares a normal area. The next section places frr0 in that area.
topic-ospf:interface:
Match the shared-link timers
  ============================

  frr0 is a broadcast link. Ze and FRR must agree on area and Hello/dead
  timers to form an adjacency: here Hello is 10 seconds, dead is 40.

  FRR calls the setting ip ospf hello-interval 10. Ze places
  hello-interval 10 under ospf interfaces interface frr0.
  The cost is the local SPF cost of this link.
topic-ospf:mismatch:
Introduce a Hello mismatch
  ==========================

  Change only Ze's Hello interval from 10 to 20 seconds.
  FRR keeps sending Hello interval 10. The mismatch rejects those
  Hellos rather than silently accepting incompatible timers.

  This is a live SSH commit on the same router, not a different lab.
topic-ospf:recovery:
Restore the matching Hello interval
  ===================================

  Put Ze's Hello interval back to 10 seconds, matching FRR.
  Leave the area, broadcast network type and dead interval unchanged.

  The repair is complete only when the neighbor is Full, its Router-LSA
  is present and the 10.255.1.2/32 route has the FRR next hop again.
topic-ospf:proof:
Trace the adjacency, database and route
  =======================================

  FRR show ip ospf neighbor maps to Ze show ospf neighbor.
  FRR show ip ospf database router maps to show ospf database router.
  FRR show ip ospf route maps to show ospf route.

  Find FRR router ID 172.29.0.2 in Full and in the Router-LSA database,
  then its loopback route through 172.29.0.2 on frr0.
topic-ospf:failure:
Make a timer disagreement visible
  =================================

  We now commit a mismatched Hello interval. The neighbor must no longer
  be Full and the route through it must disappear.

  show ospf interface detail exposes the current timers. The metric
  ze_ospf_packets_dropped_total with reason hello-interval identifies
  why incoming packets are rejected; it must increase for this failure.
topic-ospf:fix:
Repair the timer, then follow convergence
  =========================================

  The diagnostic names hello-interval, so repair that setting rather
  than restarting Ze or resetting unrelated peers.

  After the matching-timer commit, inspect neighbor, database and route
  again. A populated database alone is not proof of a usable route.
topic-ospf:recap:
A specific rejection reason and a live repair
  =============================================

  The exercise follows the same FRR neighbor through adjacency, LSDB
  and route calculation, then a Hello mismatch and recovery.

  The shown Ze process keeps its PID through all three commits.
topic-vrrp:overview:
Keep a gateway reachable through two failures
  =============================================

  Ze and keepalived share zeptrk0. VIP 203.0.113.1 belongs to VRID 12.
  Keepalived has priority 100; Ze initially has no VRRP group.

  We load two sections in one SSH candidate:

    1. Define the shared virtual gateway
    2. Lower preference when the uplink fails

  Then fail the tracked uplink AND the peer, without stopping Ze.
  Restore the peer first, then the uplink, and watch ownership move.
topic-vrrp:group:
Define the shared virtual gateway
  =================================

  Priority 200 makes Ze preferred over keepalived's 100. VRID 12 gives
  both routers virtual MAC 00:00:5e:00:01:0c for VIP 203.0.113.1.

  The rfc5798-compatible checksum interoperates with keepalived's VRRPv3.
  accept-mode true lets the non-owner answer our explicit VIP ping.
  This merges the group into the existing zeptrk0 IPv4 unit.
topic-vrrp:tracking:
Lower preference when the uplink fails
  ======================================

  Track zetrk1 and subtract 150 while it is down: 200 becomes 50.
  Keepalived at 100 then wins. Restoring zetrk1 restores priority 200.

  keepalived: track_interface { zetrk1 weight -150 }
  Ze: track { interface zetrk1 { priority-decrement 150; } }

  A weighted reduction changes preference. It does not make Ze unable
  to take over if the other router disappears.
topic-vrrp:proof:
Find the owner in both control plane and kernel
  ===============================================

  show vrrp interface name zeptrk0 reports the group, state and effective
  priority. ip address show reveals which router really owns the VIP.

  Ze should be Master at 200, with keepalived not owning the VIP.
  A real ping from the other namespace checks reachability.
topic-vrrp:failure:
Lose the uplink, not the router
  ===============================

  Bring zetrk1 down. show vrrp must name it in tracked-down and report
  effective-priority 50, while configured priority remains 200.

  Ze becomes Backup. Keepalived at 100 owns the same reachable VIP.
  The shown Ze process is still running.
topic-vrrp:takeover:
Can the less-preferred router still take over?
  ==============================================

  Stop only the keepalived peer while zetrk1 remains down.

  Ze must become Master at effective priority 50 and own the VIP.
  The kernel ownership and a ping must agree with show vrrp.
  This is failover as well as tracking, without killing the shown Ze.
topic-vrrp:fix:
Restore the peer, then the uplink
  =================================

  Restart keepalived at 100: Ze at 50 returns to Backup.
  Then restore zetrk1: Ze returns to 200 and preempts the peer.

  At every stage there must be exactly one VIP owner, with the same
  virtual MAC. Statistics show real advertisements and gratuitous ARPs.
topic-vrrp:recap:
One VIP, tracking and failover, one Ze lifetime
  ===============================================

  Priority 200 -> tracked-down Backup 50 -> peer-loss Master 50
  -> peer-restored Backup 50 -> uplink-restored Master 200.

  Both fault types keep the gateway identity and reachability checks.
  The shown Ze process is never stopped during this sequence.
topic-traffic:overview:
Find the source and application behind a burst
  ==============================================

  traffic0 joins Ze at 10.77.0.1 to a sender at 10.77.0.2.
  A real HTTP server listens on port 8080. Accounting starts absent.

  We load two sections in one live SSH candidate:

    1. Enable bounded byte accounting
    2. Observe the traffic interface

  Then establish a small ICMP/HTTP baseline, generate a heavier burst,
  identify it, stop the senders and check that the totals settle.
topic-traffic:accounting:
Enable bounded byte accounting
  ==============================

  Enable eBPF traffic accounting with source-IP attribution.
  The export interval is 250 ms, map capacity is 256 entries, and the
  stale-entry timeout is 60000 ms.

  These are cumulative byte totals, not packet payloads or live rates.
  The bounded maps limit accounting state while the router runs.
topic-traffic:interface:
Observe the traffic interface
  =============================

  Attach accounting to the existing traffic0 interface and enable its
  per-IP map. No new interface or replacement daemon is needed.

  For a MikroTik operator, /tool/torch is a familiar source/port/protocol
  attribution concept. Ze's show traffic usage reports cumulative IPv4
  byte totals instead of Torch's transmit/receive rates.
topic-traffic:proof:
Give the counters real packets to account for
  =============================================

  Send three ICMP probes and one HTTP request from traffic-peer.

  show traffic usage name traffic0 must attribute positive ingress bytes
  to source 10.77.0.2, ICMP port 0 and TCP destination port 8080.
  A configured map or a count of entries alone is not traffic evidence.
topic-traffic:failure:
Create and identify a heavier talker
  ====================================

  Start bounded ICMP and HTTP senders, then inspect two live snapshots.
  All three attributed byte totals must increase between observations.

  The filtered source metric gives the same diagnosis: 10.77.0.2 is
  sending traffic into traffic0. TCP/8080 identifies the HTTP requests;
  no packet capture or fabricated counter is involved.
topic-traffic:fix:
Stop the cause and let in-flight packets finish
  ===============================================

  Stop the senders, not Ze or the HTTP service.

  Allow at most ten seconds for a two-second window with no further
  attributed-byte increase. The next snapshots should retain their
  positive cumulative totals: recovery does not mean resetting to zero.
topic-traffic:recap:
Real attribution, bounded growth, unchanged daemon
  ==================================================

  The same eBPF interface accounted for a small baseline and a burst,
  identified its source and TCP port, then stopped growing after the
  senders stopped. No counter reset stood in for recovery.

  The shown Ze process keeps its PID throughout.
topic-ipsec:lab:
A protected host behind each router
  ===================================

  Here is our lab: this Ze initiates to a hidden Ze responder.
  10.78.1.2 and 10.78.2.2 are behind different routers.
  No VPN is configured on this router yet.

  In Junos terms, IKE authenticates the gateway and IPsec SAs
  protect the traffic. We will inspect both, then test real packets.
topic-ipsec:overview:
Build the tunnel in one live candidate
  ======================================

  Load and explain these sections, then compare and commit:
    IKE authenticates the routers
    ESP protects the packets
    Bind the peer and protected networks
    Route through the XFRM interface

  Then diagnose and repair a controlled mismatch:
    Offer an ESP cipher the far end does not accept
    Restore the shared ESP proposal
topic-ipsec:ike:
IKE authenticates the routers
  =============================

  Like a Junos security ike proposal, this group names the
  control-channel algorithms. The peer will use a lab-only PSK.
  unmatched bypass leaves unrelated lab traffic and SSH reachable.
topic-ipsec:esp:
ESP protects the packets
  ========================

  This separate proposal uses AES-256 and SHA-256 for traffic.
  Agreement on IKE alone does not guarantee an ESP Child SA.
topic-ipsec:peer:
Bind the peer and protected networks
  ====================================

  We initiate to 172.30.0.2, authenticate with a lab-only PSK,
  and protect 10.78.1.0/24 to 10.78.2.0/24 through vpn-xfrm.
  The hidden router has the reverse selectors.
topic-ipsec:xfrm:
Route through the XFRM interface
  ================================

  The new interface has if-id 42. The route sends the remote
  protected network through it. We commit these four sections
  together, without restarting the shown router.
topic-ipsec:proof:
Check negotiation, installation and traffic
  ===========================================

  Junos: show security ike security-associations, then
  show security ipsec security-associations.
  Here: show vpn ipsec sa and show vpn ipsec dataplane sa.
  Match the SPIs, ping the protected host, then read packets-in.
topic-ipsec:failure:
Change only the traffic proposal
  =================================

  The far end offers AES-256. We will offer only AES-128 for ESP.
  Authentication is unchanged. Watch the difference between an
  established IKE channel and an installed traffic-carrying SA.
topic-ipsec:mismatch:
Offer an ESP cipher the far end does not accept
  ===============================================

  This commit replaces AES-256 with AES-128 in the ESP group.
  It changes no IKE algorithm, identity or pre-shared secret.
topic-ipsec:diagnosis:
Authenticated does not mean traffic is protected
  ================================================

  The peer view has IKE but no Child SA. The log names
  NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. The kernel has no ESP SA for the tunnel.
  Empty drift means the engine and kernel agree, not that traffic flows.
topic-ipsec:restore:
Restore the shared ESP proposal
  ===============================

  Load the original AES-256 section and commit it.
  Clear this peer's SAs to negotiate again now, then prove the
  new kernel SPIs and protected traffic. Ze itself stays running.
topic-ipsec:recap:
A tunnel proven with packets, not only state
  ============================================

  The live commit created the VPN and kernel SAs.
  A deliberate ESP mismatch authenticated but protected no traffic.
  The matching proposal restored the tunnel and packets-in increased.
showcase:intro:
One running router, eight live changes
  ======================================

  Start with an ExaBGP neighbor: migrate the actual configuration.
  Then join a running BGP lab and add each feature through SSH.
  Every topic has a proof, a deliberate failure and a repair.
  This is one continuous recording, with no daemon restart.

Start with live BGP sessions
  ============================

  FRR operators know show bgp summary for peer state.
  Ze's monitor bgp keeps the view live: s sorts, q returns.
  The transit and FRR peers are established before we add features.
showcase:recap:
Configure, observe, diagnose, recover
  =====================================

  RPKI and IRR checked routes. BFD and OSPF tracked reachability.
  IPsec carried protected traffic. VRRP tracked the uplink and failed over.
  Traffic accounting identified a source. Commit confirmed restored safety.

  One router stayed running through every live commit and repair.
  Each chapter is also available as a standalone topic recording.
